title: Private VPC networking deep dive - Aurelius
summary: AE + SE walked Aurelius infra and security teams through Redwood Private VPC options: PrivateLink vs VPC endpoints, NAT/egress patterns, subnets, DNS, cross-account routing. Discussed runtime perf tradeoffs (latency vs batching), KV cache placement, quantization impacts, and benchmarking plan. Agreed next steps: send security package, run pilot benchmark in Aurelius VPC, schedule pilot kickoff.
topics: DNS / split-horizon / Route53 private hosted zones
KV cache placement and prefix caching
action_items: Maya Chen: Share Redwood security package (SOC2, ISO summary), network checklist, and sample deployment diagram by 2027-01-14
Rajesh Patel: Prepare benchmarking plan and test prompts; recommend VM/GPU specs and quantization profiles by 2027-01-18
Marcus Nguyen: Provide VPC CIDR, subnets, and contact for networking team (Diego) by 2027-01-13
Priya Das: Confirm requirements for KMS/HSM integration and egress restrictions by 2027-01-17
next_steps: Redwood to send security docs and network checklist

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-11
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rajesh Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Redwood), Lena Ortiz (CTO, Aurelius), Marcus Nguyen (Infra), Priya Das (Security), Diego Ramos (Platform)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we have about an hour, um we'll focus on the Private VPC networking stuff you flagged — PrivateLink, endpoints, NAT/egress, and then tie that back to runtime perf and KV cache. Quick intros?
[00:10] Lena Ortiz: Hi, Lena here CTO, Marcus and Priya are on for infra and security, Diego platform. We're mostly evaluating for PHI workloads so egress and KMS are big ones.
[00:22] Marcus Nguyen: yeah we want to avoid public internet egress where possible, also curious about latency overhead if you run inside our VPC vs Redwood hosted.
[00:30] Rajesh Patel: Great question. At a high level we support two private connectivity patterns: PrivateLink (interface endpoints / AWS NLB-backed) for our control plane interactions, and customer-managed VPC endpoints for data plane. For fully private with no internet egress you can use interface endpoints plus NAT in a controlled subnet for model downloads if needed.
[00:48] Priya Das: when you say control plane, do you mean telemetry and billing? Need assurance telemetry is pushed over PrivateLink only.
[00:55] Maya Chen: yes control plane (billing, metrics) can go over PrivateLink. You can opt to route all traffic to Redwood's endpoint from inside your VPC; nothing needs to touch public internet if you don't want it to. We'll share the endpoint ARNs.
[01:05] Diego Ramos: whats the perf hit for model inference when using interface endpoints? we've seen in other vendors an extra 5-20ms.
[01:12] Rajesh Patel: There's a few components. If the model runtime (inference) is colocated in your VPC—i.e., Redwood Private deployed as customer-managed nodes—the network hop is internal and latency is minimal. If using Hosted but over PrivateLink, the interface endpoint adds a small TCP/ENI hop — usually single-digit ms. More importantly, the token generation latency is dominated by GPU compute and KV cache locality and batching strategy, not the endpoint itself.
[01:34] Marcus Nguyen: can you expand on KV cache placement? we worried about cross-AZ latency if cache is in a different AZ to the serving node.
[01:40] Rajesh Patel: Absolutely. For low-latency workloads we recommend keeping KV cache colocated with the serving instance in the same AZ or same instance if using local SSD-backed cache. For multi-AZ high-availability you can replicate cache but that increases write/replication overhead and cost. Typical setup: per-AZ cache shard + sticky routing so requests hit local shard. That keeps P50/P95 down.
[02:05] Lena Ortiz: sticky routing meaning session affinity on your side or a Redwood router?
[02:10] Rajesh Patel: Redwood router can be configured for AZ-affinity; we also support affinity tokens in the request so you can pin sessions. We'll show config snippets.
[02:18] Priya Das: about egress — we have strict controls, only certain IP ranges allowed out and need to avoid unexpected DNS leaks. How does Redwood handle DNS in PrivateLink patterns?
[02:27] Maya Chen: For PrivateLink you create interface endpoints that get ENIs in your subnets. We recommend using Route53 private hosted zones and conditional forwarding so internal hostnames resolve to the endpoint. We provide a DNS suffix (e.g., private-api.redwood.example) and docs for split-horizon DNS.
[02:38] Diego Ramos: ok and for models updates/initial artifact download, do nodes reach out to public object stores?
[02:44] Rajesh Patel: Two options: 1) we can pull model artifacts from Redwood-managed stores via a peered path or signed URL over PrivateLink; 2) you can host model artifacts in your S3 and we mount with cross-account role or use presigned URLs. If you want zero egress to internet, we suggest using S3 VPC endpoints and share role access.
[02:58] Marcus Nguyen: NAT placement question — we tend to route outbound through a central NAT in a management account. Is that compatible?
[03:04] Rajesh Patel: Yes, central egress via NAT gateway or centralized egress appliance is common. Just ensure the subnet where the endpoint ENIs land has route table entries to the NAT/egress stack. If you want auditing, we recommend adding VPC flow logs and using a proxy that logs outbound connections.
[03:18] Lena Ortiz: switching to runtime perf — you mentioned batching and quantization. How big an impact does quantization have on latency and quality?
[03:25] Rajesh Patel: Quantization tradeoffs depend on model family. For many Llama-like models int8/4 quant provides 2-4x token throughput improvements with minimal quality delta for many workloads, but tail-case hallucination or instruction-following might see regressions. We recommend running evals on your prompt set. Latency per token often drops, but cold-starts for quantized kernels can add a small overhead.
[03:44] Diego Ramos: and batching — what's the recommended batch size for low latency vs high throughput?
[03:48] Rajesh Patel: If your SLO is sub-100ms per request we favor small, adaptive batches (1-8) with immediate flush policies; throughput-oriented setups allow larger batch sizes (16-64) and micro-batching. Redwood runtime uses dynamic batching: it will aggregate small requests but honor latency SLOs with priority queues. You can control batch windows per route.
[04:06] Priya Das: are there differences in autoscaling behavior for Private deployments vs Hosted? we need deterministic scaling to satisfy SLOs.
[04:12] Rajesh Patel: For Private deployments we provide autoscaling agents that work with your cluster autoscaler or our operator. Scaling triggers can be queue depth, tokens/sec, or custom metrics. We also support reserved capacity pools to avoid cold-starts and warm GPU instances.
[04:27] Marcus Nguyen: curious about cross-account PrivateLink — we run infra in a centralized account and apps in others. Can Redwood's interface endpoint be shared across accounts?
[04:34] Maya Chen: Yes, interface endpoints can be shared via endpoint services and acceptor principals. We document the required principal and allowlist flows. There's also an option to use AWS PrivateLink with an NLB in our account and accept connections from your accounts. We provide an architecture doc.
[04:50] Lena Ortiz: any gotchas on security groups for interface endpoints? we've tripped on SG blocking ephemeral ports.
[04:56] Rajesh Patel: Make sure SGs allow inbound from your app subnets on the configured ports (typically 443). For data plane we recommend stricter SGs between serving nodes and cache. If you're using cross-AZ traffic, ensure inter-AZ SG rules and NACLs don't block ephemeral ranges used by the runtime.
[05:12] Diego Ramos: about observability—can we get per-token latency traces and logs streamed to our ELK?
[05:17] Rajesh Patel: Yes, Redwood agents can forward traces and aggregated token metrics to your monitoring endpoints over PrivateLink. We can also ship logs to S3 via VPC endpoints; or you can pull them from our control plane via the secure endpoint. We'll provide sample Fluentd/Vector configs.
[05:32] Priya Das: KMS integration—do you support customer-managed keys for model encryption and logs?
[05:38] Maya Chen: Yes, support for customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS) for keys used in the Private deployment. For on-prem/HSM scenarios we support bringing your own HSM with connectors. We'll include the KMS configuration guide.
[05:48] Marcus Nguyen: Rajesh, can you walk briefly through the recommended subnet topology?
[05:52] Rajesh Patel: Sure. Recommended pattern: three tiers per AZ — public load balancer (if any), private serving subnets (no IGW), and management subnets for updates/ops with restricted egress. Put interface endpoints in the serving subnets so the control plane traffic stays local. For KV cache consider local SSD or EBS gp3 in the serving subnet; if using managed cache (Redis/Memcached) place it in private subnets with security group rules limiting access to serving nodes.
[06:13] Lena Ortiz: what about intra-AZ traffic charges if we replicate cache across AZs?
[06:17] Rajesh Patel: Cross-AZ replication does incur charges; it's visible in the infra bill. Sometimes it's cheaper to accept a slightly higher P95 and avoid replication. We'll quantify estimates in the benchmarking plan.
[06:28] Maya Chen: any performance expectations you can share? for a 4k context model with quantization and local KV cache, rough tokens/sec numbers?
[06:35] Rajesh Patel: rough ballpark: on an A100/RTX-class equivalent with int8 quant and efficient kernels you might see 200-800 tokens/sec depending on sequence length and batch. With smaller GPUs numbers vary. We'll put concrete benchmarks in the plan targeted to your prompt set.
[06:51] Diego Ramos: can we run a smoke benchmark in our VPC with a small model and your agent? what's required from our side?
[06:57] Maya Chen: Yes; we just need a peered endpoint or interface endpoint, IAM role for agent, and a subnet where the agent can run. For artifact access either S3 role or PrivateLink to our model store. We'll send the minimal network checklist.
[07:08] Marcus Nguyen: one last on DNS — we run a split-horizon with Route53, how do you avoid accidental resolution to public endpoints during failover?
[07:15] Rajesh Patel: We recommend using explicit private hosted zones with higher priority and TTLs. Also implement health checks and failover routing in Route53 and avoid reliance on public CNAMEs. Our docs include a DNS failover pattern.
[07:27] Lena Ortiz: ok let's wrap, I think we have clear items.
[07:30] Maya Chen: recap — Redwood to share security pack, network checklist, endpoint ARNs, and benchmark plan. Aurelius to share VPC details and confirm KMS requirements. We'll aim to kick off pilot week of 2027-01-20.
[07:42] Priya Das: noted. Thanks everyone.
[07:44] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up in email and post docs in the shared folder.

(Transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts and minor speaker attribution errors.)
